Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Begin with SECTION A.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you no marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Choose Picture B and say so.
2. Describe the house, the trees and the valley.
3. Link the picture to a memory: the first visit to the grandparents' home.
4. Daily life and evening stories, then the lessons learnt.
5. Conclusion: the house today.

**Model composition (526 words)**

I have chosen Picture B.

When I look at this photograph, my mind flies back to the holidays I spent at my grandparents' home in the highlands, a house very much like this one. It stands halfway up a hill, hidden among trees and shrubs, and it overlooks a wide valley that stretches towards a line of distant hills.

The main building is a low, white house with a long, gently sloping roof. Its small windows look out over the valley, and a narrow terrace runs along the front, where my grandfather used to sit with his pipe each evening. Behind it rises a second, larger building with a dark, steep roof, half buried in tall, dark green trees. Cypress trees, as straight and tall as watchmen, guard the house on every side, and thick bushes and tall grass crowd the compound so closely that the paths are almost invisible.

Beyond the garden, the land falls away in gentle slopes, patched with farms, bushes and scattered trees. Far below, a white road winds like a ribbon through the fields. On the horizon, a chain of blue hills lies under a pale sky, one behind another, until they fade into the mist.

I was ten years old when I first arrived at that house. We had travelled all day from the city, and I was tired, hungry and quite unwilling to spend the whole holiday in the countryside. Yet the next morning, when I opened the shutters and saw the valley bathed in golden light, I forgot my complaints at once. The air was cool and smelt of wet leaves and wood smoke, and somewhere below, a cock crowed to greet the day.

My days there were simple and happy. In the morning I helped my grandmother to fetch water and to feed the chickens. At noon we ate roasted corn and fresh vegetables from the garden, and in the afternoon I explored the slopes with my cousins, following narrow tracks through the bushes and listening for the sound of streams. In the evening, we sat on the terrace while my grandfather told stories about the days when the house was built, and about the wise old people who had first settled on the hill. As darkness fell, the lights of distant villages began to twinkle in the valley like fallen stars.

That house also taught me important lessons. I learnt that happiness does not depend on luxury, but on people who love us and on the beauty around us. I learnt to respect nature, because the same hills that fed us could send down mud and floods in the rainy season. Above all, I learnt that the village is not a place of the past but a source of strength, to which we must return from time to time to remember who we are.

Years have passed, and my grandparents are no longer there, but the house still stands. Whenever life in the city becomes noisy and tiring, I close my eyes and see again the white walls, the dark trees and the quiet valley. It is, for me, the most peaceful place in the world.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | A clear and sustained link with the picture chosen (named), with a precise description and a coherent development |
| Expression | 8 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate register, effective linking and a sustained, natural style |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation; paragraphs correctly marked |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing a composition that has no clear connection with the picture: the question requires one.
2. Not saying which picture was chosen, or describing both pictures superficially instead of developing one.
